title: Why Hoover Dam Is Full of Pipes
sources: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Hoover Dam FAQ (usbr.gov/lc/hooverdam/faqs/damfaqs.html) and essay 'Concrete' (usbr.gov/lc/hooverdam/history/essays/concrete.html): poured in one continuous mass, the dam's concrete would have taken about 125 years to cool and the stresses would have cracked it; instead it was built as separate blocks (columns) placed in 5-foot lifts

USBR Hoover Dam FAQ / NRMCA 'Hoover Dam' (America 250) / SpaceDaily 'Hoover Dam was cast in columns because one solid pour would take 125 years' / ENR 'Building the Hoover Dam': 582 miles of 1-inch steel pipe embedded in the concrete; river water and then ice-cold water from a refrigeration plant on site was pumped through them; once cooled, the pipes and the joints between the columns were filled with grout so the dam acts as one monolith

ACI 207.4R 'Cooling and Insulating Systems for Mass Concrete' / STRUCTURE magazine 'Mass Concreting': cement hydration releases heat; temperature differences between a hot core and a cooler surface cause thermal cracking; modern mass pours still use embedded cooling pipes (post-cooling) and replace part of the mixing water with ice (pre-cooling)

lines.text: If you pour a giant dam in one go, it stays hot for a hundred and twenty-five years.
lines.caps: If you pour a giant dam | in one go, | it stays hot | for 125 years.

lines.text: That's because concrete makes its own heat as it hardens.
lines.caps: That's because concrete | makes its own heat | as it hardens.

lines.text: The outside cools and shrinks, the hot inside doesn't, and the dam cracks.
lines.caps: The outside cools | and shrinks, | the hot inside doesn't, | and the dam cracks.

lines.text: So, at Hoover Dam, builders poured it as separate giant blocks, five feet at a time.
lines.caps: So, at Hoover Dam, | builders poured it | as separate giant blocks, | 5 feet at a time.

lines.text: But even one block was too thick to cool down.
lines.caps: But even one block | was too thick | to cool down.

lines.text: So, they buried steel pipes in every layer, five hundred eighty-two miles of them.
lines.caps: So, they buried steel pipes | in every layer, | 582 miles of them.

lines.text: First river water, then ice-cold water from a refrigeration plant, pulled the heat out.
lines.caps: First river water, | then ice-cold water | from a refrigeration plant, | pulled the heat out.

lines.text: But as the blocks cooled, they shrank, leaving thin gaps between them.
lines.caps: But as the blocks cooled, | they shrank, | leaving thin gaps | between them.

lines.text: So, workers pumped grout into the gaps and the pipes, locking it all into one solid wall.
lines.caps: So, workers pumped grout | into the gaps and the pipes, | locking it all | into one solid wall.

lines.text: You see, the real enemy of giant concrete isn't weight, it's heat.
lines.caps: You see, | the real enemy | of giant concrete | isn't weight, it's heat.

lines.text: That's why huge concrete pours today still hide cooling pipes, or even ice in the mix.
lines.caps: That's why huge concrete pours | today still hide cooling pipes, | or even ice | in the mix.
